content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to allow its own experts to review forensic images in the case and to produce documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Details below.

[關鍵背景]

In early July this year, Apple filed suit against a former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, alleging misappropriation of trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves several former employees alleged to have taken confidential material with them when they left Apple. Apple also alleges that former employee Chang Liu (劉昌) provided suggested study materials to another Apple employee before interviewing at OpenAI, while Tang Tan (陳丹) instructed Apple job candidates to bring hardware components and other materials to their interviews.

Earlier, Apple said a preliminary forensic examination of a MacBook Liu had used after leaving the company revealed he had used an Apple confidential circuit schematic to run simulations while employed at OpenAI. Apple also said the MacBook showed Liu had used a Mac mini, and the company subsequently applied for access to support the case.

OpenAI then pushed back on Apple's allegations, arguing the episode was "a mess of Apple's own making," because the company was allegedly too lax with offboarding procedures and security, making it easier for employees to inadvertently retain access to confidential material after their departure.

One dispute in the case is Apple's request to expedite discovery, which OpenAI opposes. Another is Apple's motion for an injunction to restrict OpenAI's use of its alleged trade secrets during the litigation, which could affect hardware development OpenAI is currently working on.

Apple argues that, because OpenAI is still developing its hardware products, expedited discovery is necessary since any alleged use of Apple's trade secrets could become further entangled with those products, making reversal harder down the line.

OpenAI counters that Apple has failed to show why a separate expedited discovery process is needed, and that Apple's demands are overly broad.

With the parties at an impasse, the court ordered them to file a joint submission setting out their respective positions on expedited discovery. That submission was filed last Friday and is now public.

[Apple seeks forensic images and development documents]

In the joint submission, Apple asks the court to allow its own forensic experts to directly review the forensic images the defendants' experts relied on when analysing Liu's devices, so it can determine whether Liu accessed or used Apple confidential material after leaving the company.

Apple says its forensic expert has already found "multiple significant gaps" in the opposing analysis and that its experts need direct access to the underlying material to determine whether other errors exist in the defendants' forensic analysis.

Apple's statement:

Apple's forensic expert has identified several significant gaps in the defendants' experts' analysis, including: (1) failing to find files on Liu's Mac mini that were clearly accessed and stored on it; (2) incorrectly concluding that zero-byte files or empty kMDItemLastUsedDate fields on the Mac mini meant the files had never been accessed. Allowing Apple's experts direct access to those forensic images is critical to understanding other mistakes the defendants' experts may have made.

OpenAI opposes giving Apple's experts unfettered access to the forensic images, and proposes instead using a neutral forensic expert under a procedure agreed by both sides.

Apple argues this would put it at a disadvantage, because the defendants' own forensic experts have already had direct access to the same material.

Beyond the forensic material, Apple is also pushing to expedite the production of documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including R&D materials on metal finishing, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI previously argued that its metal finishing processes were independently developed and did not use Apple's trade secrets, and that the simulations Liu ran using Apple confidential files had no connection to its forthcoming products.

Apple is now seeking the relevant development records to verify those claims. OpenAI says this is merely an attempt to "spy on a competitor."

Apple's statement:

OpenAI's statement:

The joint submission also addresses several other disputes, including:

  • Apple is further seeking forensic images of devices used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng (彭玉婷), and another OpenAI employee that contain what Apple defines as "Apple-derived information";
  • Records related to Liu's use of AI tools — the defendants previously said the forensic investigation found no evidence he used Apple confidential files on platforms such as ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Documents relating to interviews at OpenAI's consumer hardware division, including showing what materials were actually used during interviews at that division, and communications with former Apple employees;
  • OpenAI indicates there may be written interrogatories involving more than 400 former Apple employees now working at the company.

Apple is also seeking the complete LINE conversation records between Liu and Peng, including exchanges in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about his work at Apple after he left.

The defendants previously produced portions of those conversations in opposing Apple's bid for an injunction, but Apple argues it should be permitted to review the full conversations, not just the messages the defendants chose to submit.
